title: A performance-based multivariable weighting framework  for WRF parameterization-scheme selection
abstract: This study proposes a performance-based method to improve WRF climate simulation evaluation by addressing uncertainty in selecting scheme combinations. The method gives greater importance to difficult-to-simulate variables, such as precipitation and wind speed. Tested in two contrasting climate regions, it identified interpretable and well-performing model settings compared with equal weighting and established statistical weighting methods, including in the independent extreme-year test.

title: Unmasking Compensating Errors in Numerical Weather Models: A Process-Additive Neural Network Approach
abstract: arXiv:2610.19772v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work introduces a Process Additive Neural Network (PANN) framework to disentangle compensating biases in atmospheric models, where errors in different physical processes can offset each other and obscure their origins. Using a single-column model, each PANN branch represents the tendency error associated with a separate physical process, and the summed branch outputs approximate the total error relative to a reference tendency. Once trained successfully, the branch outputs are expected to provide process-level error attributions and, when averaged, estimates of process-level bias. Initial experiments focus on cloud-related processes in OpenIFS SCM case studies, where cloud and convection tendencies are strongly coupled and compensation is difficult to diagnose using standard approaches. The aim is not to replace human interpretation of physical processes, but to extend it to regimes where model complexity, process interaction, and compensating errors make direct diagnosis difficult. By providing a physically structured form of machine-learning interpretability, PANN can help connect complex model behaviour with process-level explanations. This work supports both improved understanding of compensating errors and the development of more physically consistent weather and climate models.

title: High-level, efficient ocean modeling at all scales with Oceananigans
abstract: arXiv:2502.14148v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We describe the user interface, governing equations, and numerical methods underpinning the ocean modeling software called "Oceananigans". Oceananigans development has been led by the Climate Modeling Alliance as part of a larger effort to build a trainable climate model with quantifiable uncertainty. Notably, Oceananigans is written in the Julia programming language, is optimized for GPUs, and can efficiently simulate all scales of ocean motion ranging from millimeter-scale turbulence in a small box to planetary-scale ocean circulation. We argue that this combination of capabilities is enabled by a design that combines a basic, easy-to-optimize, GPU-friendly structured finite volume algorithm exposed behind a high-level, programmable user interface. This design negotiates a dual mandate for highest-possible performance (to support state-of-the-art applications) and enhanced accessibility (to facilitate adoption and development). The dual mandate aims ultimately to accelerate the progress of Earth system science.

title: Cosmic Rays as an Interdisciplinary Earth Observation Tool: From Particle Physics and Atmospheric Processes to Geosciences and Urban Science
abstract: arXiv:2601.19265v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The exploration of cosmic rays, which are high-energy particles originating from space and the atmosphere, has historically been associated with particle physics and astrophysics. In the last 20 years, these particles have evolved into valuable tools for observing Earth's systems. This review compiles the use of cosmic rays in three primary areas: (1) particle physics and atmospheric processes, which include cosmic- ray-induced cascades, ionization, and their impact on atmospheric chemistry and radiation; (2) geosciences, where cosmogenic radionuclides assist in the dating of geological materials and cosmic-ray neutrons are used for large-scale monitoring of soil moisture and snow water equivalents; and (3) urban science, where cosmic- ray muons are employed for non-invasive subsurface imaging and, when paired with distributed sensors, serve as the basis for smart city monitoring. This review places particular emphasis on integrating these methods with remote sensing and geographic information systems (GIS), which helps close the persistent scale gap between point measurements and satellite observations, thereby enabling three-dimensional digital representations of subsurfaces. This review concludes by discussing data standards, their integration into operational Earth observation workflows, and future research directions.

title: KNOU-Flood: Advancing global streamflow forecasting with lead-aware probabilistic machine learning
abstract: arXiv:2610.20640v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Global streamflow forecasting supports flood preparedness, yet data-driven models trained on reanalysis lose skill when driven by operational forecasts, increasingly so with lead time. AIFL addresses this shift with a two-stage transfer-learning recipe and a deterministic LSTM, but it feeds one forecast lead time into the whole input window and gives no uncertainty. We ask how far this open recipe can be extended without changing its recurrent core. KNOU-Flood keeps a single-layer LSTM and the two-stage training and changes the information around it: a longer input window (424 days), lead-aware forecast inputs, GraphCast as a second forecast source next to ECMWF HRES, and a latent-noise ensemble trained with the fair CRPS. We compare against a re-implementation of the AIFL recipe (its code is not public) under identical data, stations, splits and metrics. Our contributions are threefold. First, over three seeds and 2,099 test basins (2021-2023), KNOU-Flood reaches a median KGE' of 0.65 at LT1 and 0.48 at LT10 against 0.62 and 0.34, with significant gains at all ten lead times under two scoring protocols, also against a 1024-unit baseline and on held-out basins (one seed each). Second, identical weights give an LT10 KGE' of 0.18 or 0.34 depending on how forecasts are fed, so much of the lead-time decay reported for AIFL is an input-protocol effect; the probabilistic head contributes most to the gain, followed by the raw GraphCast channels, the longer window and mixed fine-tuning. Third, the ensembles reach lower CRPS than probabilistic versions of the baseline, are nearly calibrated with inference-time dropout, and detect 1.5- and 2-year floods better than all baselines; the benefit for rarer floods depends on the seed, and an exploratory tail-weighted variant improves 10-year and larger events. KNOU-Flood is a controlled extension of an open recipe, not a new architecture.

title: Changes in southeastern Pacific Ocean cloud fractions: cloud radiative effects and cloud controlling factors
abstract: Abstract Clouds play a critical role in Earth’s radiative balance through their radiative effects. Recent studies suggest that the current planetary energy imbalance is associated with a reduction in global albedo, largely resulting from decreases in cloud fraction. However, the southeastern Pacific Ocean, where maritime stratocumulus clouds dominate off the west coast of South America, shows increasing albedo associated with enhanced low cloud cover. In this study, PATMOS-x v6.0, a satellite-based long-term climate data record derived from the AVHRR instruments aboard polar orbiting satellites, and CERES EBAF are used to investigate changes in cloud fraction and albedo, respectively. Both datasets show increases in anomalies of water cloud amount (1.21%∙decade −1 ) and albedo (0.25%∙decade −1 ), and these variables have been strongly correlated since 2000. Applying the cloud-controlling factors framework using 6 atmospheric variables from the ERA5 reanalysis dataset and ridge regression method indicates that these changes are primarily driven by an increase in estimated inversion strength (0.31 K∙decade −1 ). The slope between water cloud amount and EIS anomalies is 2.81%∙K −1 from Pv6.0 and 2.37%∙K −1 from ridge regression model. The increase in EIS is associated with enhanced lower tropospheric stability, resulting from a decrease in surface temperature (−0.07 K∙decade −1 ) and an increase in atmospheric temperature at 700 hPa (0.24 K∙decade −1 ) over the last four decades. The long-term decrease in surface potential temperature is closely associated with ENSO variability, whereas the increase in potential temperature at 700 hPa is incompatible with an ENSO-only explanation, implying that other thermodynamic or circulation changes are contributing to enhanced lower tropospheric stability.

title: Disentangling forced and internal components in observed climate evolution using spatiotemporal deep learning
abstract: arXiv:2610.28219v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Attribution of observed historical climate evolution to externally forced change and internal variability is fundamental to understanding climate change and evaluating climate models. Yet such attribution remains challenging because the forced response is intertwined with internal variability in observations. Here, we develop a convolutional long short-term memory network (ConvLSTM) to disentangle these two components. Trained and evaluated using large-ensemble simulations from multiple climate models, ConvLSTM consistently outperforms existing model-based, statistical, and machine-learning approaches. Applying ConvLSTM to observations reveals an evolving spatial pattern of the forced response and substantial contributions from internal variability to recent multidecadal climate trends. For several key climate features whose attribution remains debated, ConvLSTM indicates that internal variability amplified the forced reversal of Atlantic interhemispheric temperature asymmetry, dominated the observed La Ni\~na-like warming pattern over the equatorial Pacific and the associated precipitation decline over southwestern North America since 1980, and modulated Arctic amplification around its nearly constant threefold forced value. Comparison between the ConvLSTM-estimated and model-simulated forced responses reveals broadly consistent patterns but also important discrepancies, with climate models simulating stronger Northern Hemisphere warming, weaker subtropical high intensification, and smaller land precipitation declines. Overall, ConvLSTM provides a robust framework for attributing historical climate evolution and evaluating the fidelity of climate models

title: Nonlinear Amplification of Summer Extreme Heat Events in Northeast China and Mongolia by the Preceding Winter Northeast Pacific Cold Blob and Spring Indo-Pacific Warm Pool SST
abstract: Abstract Summer extreme heat events pose severe risks to society and ecosystems. This study reveals a significant synergistic effect between the preceding winter negative Northeast Pacific sea surface temperature anomalies (nNEP SSTA), known as the “cold blob”, and spring negative Indo-Pacific Warm Pool SST anomalies (nIPWP SSTA), that intensifies summer heat extremes in Northeast China and Mongolia. When co-occurring, these factors nonlinearly amplify heat events far beyond their individual linear effects. The mechanism for this synergistic effect involves a series of coupled oceanic and atmospheric bridges. The two factors jointly generate spring anomalous westerlies that sustain the nNEP SSTA into summer via the Wind-Evaporation-SST feedback. This persistent summer anomaly triggers eastward propagating Rossby waves energy, establishing a strong local anticyclone and increased atmospheric thickness over Northeast China and Mongolia, which directly increases the temperature of the atmospheric layer and favors extreme heat events. Furthermore, this circulation induces soil moisture deficits, further intensifying the heat through soil moisture feedback. These nonlinear processes are confirmed by General circulation model experiments. These findings highlight the importance of the synergistic influence of these remote SST anomalies for the prediction of summer heat extremes over Northeast China and Mongolia.

title: Forecasting carbon-risk hotspots ahead of the extreme 2026 El Ni\~no
abstract: arXiv:2610.16714v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A potentially super El Ni\~no is forecasted in 2026, raising the need to anticipate land carbon-cycle risks before its impacts unfold. We develop a prospective early-warning framework that uses dynamic global vegetation models driven by an ensemble of ECMWF seasonal climate forecasts and machine-learning burned area predictions. Forecasts indicate a $0.23 \pm 0.21$ PgC reduction in global net biome productivity in the second half of 2026, with hotspots of sink weakening in eastern South America and elevated fire risk in Southeast Asia.

title: PrecipCorrDiff: A Deep Learning Framework for Generating 0.0625$^\circ$ High-Resolution IMD Gridded Precipitation Data
abstract: arXiv:2610.19994v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-resolution precipitation datasets are essential for weather forecasting, hydrological modeling, and climate risk assessment, yet observation-based gridded products often lack the spatial detail required for regional applications. Here we present PrecipCorrDiff, a diffusion-based downscaling framework built by modifying the original corrector diffusion based archetecture that incorporates a customized loss function and a multi-scale residual generation strategy to improve the precipitation especially the representation of extremes. PrecipCorrDiff generates 0.0625{\deg} resolution India Meteorological Department (IMD) precipitation fields from 0.25{\deg} gridded data while preserving precipitation statistics and reconstructing fine-scale spatial variability. Validation against independent IMD station observations, comparing the proposed framework with the SRGAN-based model and the original CorrDiff model, indicates that the proposed framework substantially improves the representation of spatial precipitation patterns, rainfall intensity distributions, and extreme rainfall events, while eliminating the systematic negative bias present in the previously developed SRGAN-based model. Across four climatologically distinct homogeneous Indian monsoon regions, PrecipCorrDiff reproduces observed precipitation characteristics with near-zero spatial bias, demonstrating the potential of diffusion-based downscaling for generating physically consistent, high-resolution precipitation datasets for hydrological, meteorological, and climate applications.

title: Improved Precipitation Variability in the Community Atmosphere Model through Implementation of a Neural-Network Deep Convection Scheme
abstract: arXiv:2610.20405v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional deep convection schemes remain a primary source of uncertainty in global climate models, yet replacing them with data-driven alternatives while maintaining physical consistency and numerical stability is an open challenge. We present a hybrid configuration of the Community Atmosphere Model version 6 (CAM6), in which a fully connected deep neural network replaces the Zhang-McFarlane deep convection scheme (ZM), while radiation, turbulence, and other cloud processes are left unchanged. The network is trained on output from a storm-resolving global model - the global System for Atmospheric Modeling (gSAM) - using a coarse-graining approach to derive subgrid-scale convective fluxes and tendencies. This data-driven parameterization is ported to CAM6 and found to run stably for more than a decade while conserving energy and moisture. It produces a broadly realistic climatology without retuning the remaining parameterizations. Relative to the default Zhang-McFarlane scheme, the neural network parameterization substantially improves some long-standing model deficiencies. In particular, the biases in light precipitation and extreme precipitation are markedly reduced, and the diurnal cycle of tropical land precipitation shifts from a spurious midday peak over many regions to the observed late-afternoon peak. These results support targeted ML-based convection schemes as a viable path toward reducing systematic model errors in next-generation climate models.

title: Quantitative Reconstruction of Late Miocene Monsoon‐Driven Climate and Hydrology in the Himalayan Foreland, Nepal
abstract: Abstract The Late Miocene was a critical interval in the evolution of the South Asian monsoon system and the Himalayan foreland. This study presents a quantitative paleoclimatic reconstruction based on fossil leaf assemblages from the Lower (10.5–9.2 Ma) and Middle (9.2–7.0 Ma) Siwalik sediments of the Daldale section, western Nepal, using the Climate Leaf Analysis Multivariate Program (CLAMP). The reconstructed mean annual temperatures are 22.2 ± 2.3°C for the Lower Siwalik and 21.5 ± 2.3°C for the Middle Siwalik, with corresponding cold month mean temperatures of 15.4 ± 3.3°C and 15.0 ± 3.3°C. Mean annual precipitation ranges from 228 ± 48 to 238 ± 48 cm, and the annual vapor pressure deficit remains close to 6 ± 2 hPa, indicating persistently warm and humid monsoon‐influenced conditions throughout the study interval. Although several climatic variables exhibit coherent directional trends, including slightly lower temperatures, reduced rainfall concentration during the wettest months, and subtle changes in seasonal moisture availability in the Middle Siwalik, these differences largely overlap within the uncertainties of the CLAMP reconstructions. Consequently, the Daldale record indicates broad climatic stability rather than a major climatic transition between the Lower and Middle Siwalik intervals within the studied section. The study provides the first quantitative paleoclimatic benchmark for the Daldale Siwalik succession and demonstrates that climatic responses within the Himalayan foreland were spatially heterogeneous, with western Nepal maintaining persistently humid conditions despite broader regional environmental changes.

title: On the theoretical limitations of joint inversion for basal slipperiness and effective viscosity in ice-flow models
abstract: In this study, we investigate the ability to extract information about ice viscosity at the same as basal slipperiness in the inversion procedure of large-scale ice-sheet models. This is an essential part of the initialisation of many large-scale computational ice-sheet models. However, there is a lack of consensus on whether a joint inversion is possible to determine these fields. We present a theoretical framework to better understand the factors influencing the retrieval.

title: Can AI Forecast the Extremes? Evaluating Probabilistic Weather Models on Tropical Cyclones
abstract: arXiv:2610.22077v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Weather prediction is undergoing an important shift, with data-driven AI models outperforming leading numerical weather prediction systems on average at a fraction of the computational cost. Yet, whether this success extends to extreme events remains contested. Earlier evaluations have exposed important shortcomings, but have largely focused on deterministic models and metrics, leaving the capabilities of the latest probabilistic models less understood. We conduct an extensive benchmark of tropical cyclone forecasting, comparing GenCast, FourCastNet 3, and FGN with ECMWF's operational physics-based ensemble, IFS-ENS. We develop a suite of probabilistic metrics and diagnostic analyses to assess cyclone tracking, intensity biases, uncertainty, and the wind-pressure relationship that characterizes storm structure. We find that, despite remaining limitations in intensity and ensemble spread, leading AI models substantially outperform IFS-ENS in cyclone tracking: FGN achieves better probabilistic location scores for 90% of evaluated storms in 2025. Further analyses reveal model-specific failure modes and suggest a lingering influence of pretraining data, pointing to opportunities for targeted improvement. Nonetheless, these results suggest that AI models are capable of capturing physical relationships that remain predictive well beyond typical weather conditions, motivating further investigation into how these capabilities emerge and how to strengthen them.

title: Indian Ocean Dipole Impacts on Autumn Heat and Early-Winter Precipitation over the Arabian Peninsula
abstract: Abstract The Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) exerts a season-spanning influence on Arabian Peninsula (AP) climate, modulating both autumn (September–November, SON) heat and early-winter (October–December, OND) precipitation. During positive IOD, the southern AP warms in SON via a radiative pathway: anomalous low-level moisture transport enhances the greenhouse effect, strengthening downward longwave radiation and diabatic heating. As conditions cool into OND, the IOD’s influence pivots to precipitation. Positive IOD amplifies OND precipitation through two mechanisms: a low-level moisture conveyor leads to convergence-dominated precipitation along the southwestern coast, while a strengthened subtropical jet interacts with this moistening environment in the northeast. In contrast, negative IOD features weaker, spatially distinct SON cooling centered over the northern AP, primarily from cold-air advection, and broadly suppressed OND precipitation. These seasonal mean shifts would alter the probability of high-impact weather. On synoptic timescales, the enhanced moisture during positive IOD can first radiatively amplify heatwaves and then fuel extreme precipitation within days. This dual fingerprint clarifies the IOD’s role in AP climate variability and provides a physical basis for assessing compound heat-rainfall hazards in a warming world.

title: Tongji-GMMG2025C: A High-Resolution Global Gravity Field Solution Integrated from Heterogeneous Gravity Data via a Grid-based VCE Method
abstract: Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) We developed a new high-resolution global gravity field model by integrating satellite, marine, terrestrial, airborne, polar, and topographic gravity information. The model substantially improves gravity estimation accuracy in coastal, polar, and data-sparse regions. Accuracy improves by 9 %–24 % within 10 km of the coastline and by approximately 40 % over Antarctica. The dataset can be used for geodesy, oceanography, and other Earth science applications.

title: Improving photosynthate allocation dynamic simulations  of crops under water stress conditions
abstract: This study improves the Agro-C model to better represent how crops respond to changing soil moisture. The updated model adjusts carbon allocation between roots and leaves according to soil moisture and growth stage, and also accounts for leaf aging under water stress. Tests with field data for maize and wheat showed better predictions of plant growth above and below ground. The results can improve estimates of crop production and soil carbon storage under future drought and climate change.

title: Improving snow simulations through improved representations of vegetation conditions: insights from high resolution simulations over California
abstract: Most hydrological models tend to underestimate snow over the mountainous southwestern US. This may result from uncertainties in precipitation forcing and/or inadequate representation of snow–vegetation interactions, particularly canopy interception and shading. Through model experiments, we demonstrate how downscaled meteorological forcing and improved vegetation representation can improve snow simulations over the southwestern US.

title: TRAILS – a novel framework for time-height-resolved attribution of long-range transported wildfire smoke
abstract: This research introduces a new method that combines model simulations with satellite observations to attribute the influence of wildfire smoke on an airmass. By dynamically determining the height of smoke plumes, we overcome a key limitation of earlier fixed reception-height approaches. This advancement is crucial for improving our understanding of how wildfire emissions influence cloud formation and the broader Earth's climate system.

title: Meso-NH-ISO v1.0: a water stable isotopologue scheme in the non-hydrostatic mesoscale atmospheric model Meso-NH – application to a 2D West African squall line
abstract: We implemented water stable isotopologues in the non-hydrostatic mesoscale atmospheric model Meso-NH. We validated this isotopic version (Meso-NH-ISO) with a simulation of a well-documented squall line in the Sahel region. In future works, simulations with Meso-NH-ISO will be done on real cases of cyclones or squall lines. The goal is to better interpret and quantify isotopic observations on the field in terms of atmospheric processes that drive development and intensity of those thunderstorms.

title: A Lagrangian particle tracking framework for the  super-droplet method in SCALE-SDM 5.2.6-2.3.1:  implementation and computational evaluation
abstract: We developed and tested a way to trace selected cloud particles in a simulation, including how they grow and merge. One run identifies particles that meet chosen conditions, and a second reconstructs only their saved histories. In a three-dimensional test, the saved data were estimated to be one-fifth of what would be needed to keep all particle histories. Larger reductions are possible when fewer particles are selected, making such studies more practical in large simulations.

title: Development and validation of ARMS-gb v2.0: extending fast radiative transfer modeling capability to all-sky conditions  for ground-based microwave radiometer retrievals
abstract: Ground-based microwave instruments can continuously observe the lower atmosphere, but clouds make their measurements harder to use. We improved a computer model so that it represents how cloud and rain particles affect these observations, and tested it with six months of measurements from two sites in China. The updated model performed better under cloudy conditions without rain, supporting more reliable use of these observations in atmospheric monitoring and weather forecasting.

title: HTAP3-OPNS: ozone, PM, nitrogen and sulphur deposition – multi-model experiments to support the revision of the CLRTAP Gothenburg Protocol
abstract: Air pollution travels across continents, meaning emissions in one region can affect air quality far away. To better understand this, scientists from many groups are planning to run coordinated computer simulations of the atmosphere. By comparing results across models and emission scenarios, the planned study will show how pollution moves between regions and which sources matter most, helping governments design more effective air quality policies.

title: Optimization of the fast layer transmittance algorithm in RTTOV v13.1 for strong water vapor absorption channels of the FY-3F HIRAS-II instrument using LBLRTM v12.11
abstract: To enhance atmospheric transmittance accuracy in strong water vapor absorption bands, this study proposes an optimized scheme for the fast transmittance algorithm applied to the Hyperspectral Infrared Atmospheric Sounder-II. It introduces a transmittance threshold for sample selection and a weighted least squares regression with transmittance weighting. Validation against line-by-line models and observations shows significant improvements in forward model accuracy and stability at 6.7 μm.

title: A preliminary study on a synergistic assimilation scheme for multi-band satellite soil moisture data
abstract: Accurate soil moisture data is essential for predicting weather. This study examined how observations from three satellites can be combined to improve land-surface simulations. While each satellite helps, their value changes with vegetation type. Merging these data sources gives a more reliable estimate of soil wetness, especially in central and western China. This approach strengthens soil-water monitoring and supports more dependable climate forecasting.
